```{r}
#| warning: false
library(survival)
```

## Learning Objectives

- Identify valid methods to compare Cox models
- Interpret concordance


## Lesson

Cox regression models are fit with "partial" likelihood,
which allows us to use likelihood-based methods to compare them.
This includes the AIC, BIC, and likelihood ratio test.

```{r}
d_dr <- diabetic
d_dr <- d_dr[d_dr$eye == "left", ]
```

For example, let's compare these two interaction models
using the diabetic retinopathy data.

```{r}
#| echo: true
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ trt * laser,
                data = d_dr)
mod_02 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ trt + trt:laser,
                data = d_dr)
AIC(mod_01)
AIC(mod_02)
BIC(mod_01)
BIC(mod_02)
anova(mod_01,
      mod_02,
      test = "LRT")
```

The simpler model has a lower AIC and lower BIC, and the likelihood ratio
test is not significant,
indicating that the simpler model is better.

Since the Cox proportional hazards model doesn't estimate a baseline hazard,
we can't use it to generate predicted values.
This means we can't use a training-test set split or cross-validation
to compare the performance of Cox models.
However, there is another way to kinda-sorta get at prediction accuracy.
If we look at the output for the two models above, we see something
called "Concordance".

```{r}
summary(mod_01)
summary(mod_02)
```

Concordance is a value between 0 and 1.
It's interpreted as a probability.
The concordance for model 1 is 0.656,
meaning that in 65.6% of randomly-selected pairs of observations,
the observation with the higher hazard has the shorter survival time.

You might be thinking, "How do you estimate concordance in the presence
of censoring?"
Good question.
In the presence of censoring, it's not necessarily possible to determine
which of two observations had the shorter survival time.
This has led to a fair number of publications on the correct way
to estimate concordance.
We're not going to get into the specifics;
it's more important to me that you know how to interpret the result.

It's also worth noting that the concordance estimates above are
for the data set that was used to estimate the model,
so they're inflated.
Again, accounting for this can be complicated, so I don't want to get into
details.


## Problems

### Problem 1

Can you use the likelihood ratio test to compare any two Cox models?
Justify your answer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

No.
The models still need to be nested,
just like for any other likelihood ratio test.

:::

### Problem 2

What measure of performance did we cover in logistic regression
that's an analog of concordance?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The AUC, also known as the "probability of superiority"
or "common language effect size".
The AUC is the probability that a randomly-selected observation
with an outcome of 1 will have a higher fitted value
than a randomly-selected observation with an outcome of 0.

:::
